modules.name: Events
modules.header:
Reading a document as a stream of events, without building a tree.
The tree is convenient and it is also the thing that makes a large document expensive: a gigabyte of JSON
becomes several gigabytes of nodes, and a program that only wants the third field of each record pays for all
of it. Streaming trades random access for constant memory — events arrive in document order, once, and the
caller keeps only what it wants.
The buffer here grows only as far as the largest single token requires, not as far as the document. An array
of ten million small numbers streams in a few hundred bytes; only a single enormous string forces the buffer
up, and the string limit is what bounds that.
Nesting is tracked so that structural mistakes are still caught — a closing brace against an open bracket is
refused here exactly as it would be by the tree parser, because a streaming reader that accepted malformed
structure would push the problem onto every caller.

modules.name: Lexer
modules.header:
Turning JSON text into tokens, under limits a caller sets.
The limits are the point of having a separate lexing stage at all. JSON is a recursive format read from
untrusted input more often than almost anything else, and every one of its failure modes is a resource
exhaustion rather than a parse error: a document of ten thousand open brackets exhausts a recursive parser's
stack before any bracket closes, a string with no closing quote consumes a whole file, and an array of a
hundred million elements exhausts memory while remaining perfectly well-formed. None of those is malformed
JSON. All of them are refusals a caller has to be able to configure, so the limits live in a value passed in
rather than in constants compiled here.
The lexer never allocates. A string token points into the input and reports whether it needs unescaping, so a
document whose strings hold no escapes — which is most of them — is parsed without copying any of them.

modules.name: Parser
modules.header:
Parsing a document into a value tree.
The recursion is bounded by the depth limit rather than by the stack, which is the only way a recursive
descent parser can safely read untrusted input: the check happens before the call, so a document designed to
exhaust the stack is refused while there is still stack left to refuse it with.
Duplicate object names are rejected by default. RFC 8259 says their behaviour is unpredictable and leaves
implementations to choose, which means a document with duplicates means different things to different
readers — and that difference has been used to smuggle one value past a validator and a different one to the
consumer behind it. Refusing is the only choice that cannot be exploited that way, so it is the default; the
alternatives exist because some real documents contain duplicates and someone has to read them.

modules.name: Value
modules.header:
What a JSON value is, and the one part of it the specification refuses to pin down.
RFC 8259 says a number is a sequence of digits with an optional fraction and exponent, and then says
implementations may set whatever limits they like on range and precision. That is the whole of it: JSON has no
integer type, no float type, and no stated precision, so every parser decides for itself and they disagree.
A parser that turns everything into a double silently corrupts an identifier past 2^53 — which is how a
Twitter status id became a different status id in a great deal of software.
So a number here keeps its text, and answers questions about itself from that. It reports whether it fits an
integer, whether it fits a float, and what it is exactly; a caller asks for the shape it needs and is told if
the value does not fit rather than being handed something close. The text is also what makes round-tripping
exact: a document read and written back keeps its numbers as they were written.

modules.name: Writer
modules.header:
Writing a value back out, compactly or for a human.
Two things here are not negotiable. Strings are escaped exactly as RFC 8259 requires and no more: the quote,
the backslash and every control character below space, using the short escapes where they exist and a
four-digit form otherwise. The solidus is *not* escaped, though many writers do it — it is legal either way,
and escaping it makes output differ from every other writer's for no benefit.
And a non-finite number cannot be written, because JSON has no way to spell one. A writer that emits `NaN` or
`Infinity` produces something that is not JSON and that other parsers reject, which turns a computation
problem into an interoperation problem somewhere far away. Refusing is the only honest answer; a caller who
has a non-finite value has to decide what it means, and only the caller can.
Failures are the ones every writer in this workspace reports, which is what lets a JSON document be written
into anything a `TextWriter` reaches without a translation at the seam. This used to be a status enum of its
own with one case, `Failed`, standing for everything a destination could say — so a buffer that was simply full
and a stream that had died arrived identically, and a caller who could have written the document somewhere
larger had no way to know that was the problem. What the destination said now travels unchanged. A non-finite
number is `ValueOutOfRange`, which is what that case is for: the value is perfectly good and the requested form
cannot hold it.

doc.summary: Why reading stopped, positioned, or `none` while nothing has gone wrong.
doc.markdown:
Why reading stopped, positioned, or `none` while nothing has gone wrong.
This is what a caller asks after `Next` reports `Error`. A lexical refusal carries the lexer's own reason
inside it rather than in a second call, so a caller holding the failure is holding all of it. The offset
counts bytes from the start of the document, however many times the buffer has been refilled. A source that
failed is reported as `Source`, and what it reported is on `SourceError`.
doc.returns: the failure, positioned at the byte of the document the reader stopped on, or `none`

doc.summary: What the source reported when reading it failed, or `none` when it has not failed.
doc.markdown:
What the source reported when reading it failed, or `none` when it has not failed.
The end of the stream is not a failure and is never reported here; any other `IoError` from the source's
`Read` stops the reader, makes `Next` report `Error` and `Failure` report `Source`, and is kept here
unchanged, so a caller can tell a document that is malformed from a stream that broke.
doc.returns: the source's failure, or `none`

doc.summary: Why parsing stopped, and where.
doc.markdown:
Why parsing stopped, and where.
Failure-only: there is no case meaning nothing went wrong, because a parse that did not fail hands back a
document instead. Every case carries the zero-based byte offset into the input where the parser stopped, which
is the first thing anybody debugging a document asks for and used to live in a separate structure that a caller
had to remember to read.

cases.name: Lexical
cases.doc:
The lexer refused the input, for the reason carried. Nested rather than reported beside this, so a caller
holding the failure cannot be holding half of it.

cases.name: Unexpected
cases.doc: A token that cannot appear where it did.

cases.name: Truncated
cases.doc: The document ended in the middle of a value.

cases.name: TrailingContent
cases.doc: Text after the end of the top-level value. The offset is where that text begins.

cases.name: DuplicateName
cases.doc: An object contained the same name twice, under the rejecting policy. The offset is the second occurrence.

cases.name: TooDeep
cases.doc: Containers nested deeper than the limit allowed.

cases.name: TooManyEntries
cases.doc: A container held more entries than the limit allowed.

cases.name: OutOfMemory
cases.doc: The allocator refused.

cases.name: BadSurrogate
cases.doc:
A `\u` escape naming half of a surrogate pair with no valid partner. JSON's escapes are UTF-16, and a lone
surrogate is not a character; the offset is the escape that has no partner.

cases.name: Source
cases.doc:
The stream a `JsonEventReader` reads from failed with something other than its end. Only a streaming reader
reports this; the source's own `IoError` is kept on the reader, through `JsonEventReader::SourceError`.

doc.summary: Where in the input parsing stopped.

doc.summary: Parses the whole document and returns its top-level value, or why it could not.
doc.markdown:
Parses the whole document and returns its top-level value, or why it could not.
Anything after that value is `TrailingContent` — a document is one value, and two concatenated ones are
not a document however well-formed each is.
A failure gives back nothing at all. Whatever had been built when the parser stopped is released here, which
is the only place that can be done once: an array that failed at its third element owns two, and handing
those back beside an error would leave a caller holding a document that is not one.
Fails with any case of `JsonParseError`, positioned at the byte where parsing stopped.
doc.returns: the document, or the failure that stopped it

doc.summary: Parses `input` into a value, rejecting duplicate names.
doc.markdown:
Parses `input` into a value, rejecting duplicate names.
The default limits apply. A failure gives back the reason and its position and no value at all, so a document
that is not a document cannot be mistaken for one that is — which the old shape allowed, since it answered a
refused parse with `null`, and `null` is a document.
Fails with any case of `JsonParseError`, positioned at the byte where parsing stopped.
doc.returns: the document, or the failure that stopped it

doc.markdown:
Parses `input` under chosen limits and a chosen duplicate-name policy.
The long form of `Parse`, for a caller who needs something other than the defaults. The policy is a
parameter rather than a mutable setting on a shared parser, so two documents read under different policies
in the same program cannot influence one another.
Fails with any case of `JsonParseError`, positioned at the byte where parsing stopped. A limit that the document
exceeds arrives as `TooDeep` or `TooManyEntries` from the parser, or nested inside `Lexical` when it was the
lexer that measured it.

Reports `false` when this is not an array or the allocator refused; `value` is consumed either way, so
a caller does not have to decide who owns it on failure.

members.signature: pub func Insert(self: &var JsonValue, name: String, value: JsonValue) -> bool

doc.summary: Appends a member to an object, taking ownership of both name and value.
doc.markdown:
Appends a member to an object, taking ownership of both name and value.
The order members are added in is the order they are kept and written, which is what makes a document
round-trip recognisably. Nothing here rejects a duplicate name — that policy lives in the parser, where
the caller can choose it.
doc.returns: whether the member was added

doc.summary: The element at `index`, borrowed, or null when there is none.
doc.markdown: The element at `index`, borrowed, or null when there is none.
doc.returns: the element at `index`, or null when there is none

doc.summary: The value of the member named `name`, borrowed, or null when there is none.
doc.markdown:
The value of the member named `name`, borrowed, or null when there is none.
With duplicate names present — which only a permissive parser policy allows — this finds the first,
since that is the one a reader encounters.
doc.returns: the first member with that name, or null when there is none

doc.summary: The member at `index`, borrowed, or null when there is none.
doc.markdown: The member at `index`, borrowed, or null when there is none.

members.name: RemoveFirst
members.signature: pub func RemoveFirst(self: &var JsonValue, name: StringView) -> bool

doc.summary: Removes the first member named `name`, if there is one.
doc.markdown:
Removes the first member named `name`, if there is one.
Used by the duplicate-name policy that keeps the last occurrence: dropping the earlier one is what keeps
the object a map rather than a list that happens to repeat itself.
The members after it are popped and pushed back rather than shifted, because shifting would move
owning values around inside the vector, and a move out of a container is the one thing the ownership
rules will not allow silently. Duplicates are rare enough that the cost never matters.
doc.returns: whether a member with that name was removed

doc.summary: Releases everything this value owns.
doc.markdown:
Releases everything this value owns.
Written out rather than left to the compiler, because a value owns its strings and its children own
theirs: the recursion here is the shape of the document, and stating it makes the ownership of a nested
tree something a reader can check.

doc.summary: How deep a document may nest before the writer refuses.
doc.markdown:
How deep a document may nest before the writer refuses.
The writer descends recursively, so this bounds its own stack rather than the document's shape. It is far past
the parser's default depth, which is what actually decides whether a document of this size can exist: a tree
built in memory rather than parsed is the only way to reach this at all.

doc.summary: How a document should be laid out.
doc.markdown: How a document should be laid out.

doc.markdown: The compact style: no whitespace anywhere. What a document on a wire should be.

items.name: WriteEscaped
items.signature: pub func WriteEscaped(writer: &var TextWriter, text: char8[..]) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes the escaped form of `text`, including its surrounding quotes.
doc.markdown:
Writes the escaped form of `text`, including its surrounding quotes.
Escapes exactly what the standard requires: the quote, the backslash, and every control character below
space. Bytes above that pass through unchanged, so a UTF-8 document stays UTF-8 rather than being expanded
into escapes — which is legal but makes output several times larger for no gain.
Reports whatever the destination reported, stopping at the first refusal, so a destination that has already
refused something is not written to again and a partly written string is not followed by its closing quote.

params.name: text
params.markdown: the UTF-8 bytes to escape and write

doc.returns: success when the whole quoted string was accepted

items.name: WriteValue
items.signature: pub func WriteValue(writer: &var TextWriter, value: &JsonValue, style: JsonStyle) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes `value` to `writer` in the given style.
doc.markdown:
Writes `value` to `writer` in the given style.
The value is borrowed and nothing is allocated: the document writes itself into the destination as it is
walked. A number is written as the text it was read with, which is what keeps an identifier past 2^53 coming
back as itself.
Reports whatever the destination reported, unchanged, so a buffer that is merely full stays distinguishable
from a stream that has died — and stops at the first refusal rather than writing the rest of a document into a
destination that has already said no. Reports `ValueOutOfRange` for a number JSON cannot spell, and for a
document nested past `MaximumWriteDepth`.

params.name: value
params.markdown: the document to write, borrowed for the call

doc.returns: success when the whole document was accepted
